speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Over the past few years, Government agencies have worked closely with banks to put in place measures to safeguard the public from scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, we have the Money Lock, which allows bank customers to set aside a portion of their funds in their bank accounts that cannot be transferred digitally; and we also have the Kill Switch, which allows bank customers to suspend their accounts quickly if they suspect that their bank accounts have been compromised.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Despite the safeguards and extensive public education efforts, we still see a high number of scams involving self-effected transfers, where individuals willingly transfer monies to scammers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These include government official impersonation scams, investment scams and Internet love scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such scams rely on social engineering and prey on respect for authority, greed and the human desire for companionship and love.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In some cases, the Police have observed that the victims were so taken in by the scammers' deceit, that they refused to believe that they were being scammed, despite being repeatedly advised by family, friends, their bank and even the Police.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: By the time these victims realised the truth, the scammers had siphoned their monies out of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In a love scam case, a 64-year-old female victim befriended the scammer on a social media platform and entered into an online relationship with him.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The scammer claimed to be working on an offshore oil rig project outside Singapore and told the victim that once his project was completed, he could come to Singapore to marry her.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Over the course of about two years, the scammer repeatedly asked for money from the victim, claiming it was to buy equipment for the project or to pay his workers' salaries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Each time, the victim transferred the money to various bank accounts designated by the scammer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Despite attempts by the Police and her family to convince her that she was being scammed, she continued to make money transfers to the scammer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It was only after multiple engagements by the Police that the victim was finally convinced that she was being scammed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: And by that time, unfortunately, the victim had already lost about $400,000 to the scammer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In another case and this is an example of a love and investment scam, a 33-year-old male victim met the scammer on an online dating platform.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The scammer slowly gained the victim's trust, eventually deceiving the victim into believing that they were in a relationship.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The scammer then introduced the victim to a fake investment opportunity promising substantial profits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Believing that the investment opportunity was legitimate, the victim made several transactions to multiple bank accounts on the scammer's instructions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The transactions amounted to a total of $200,000.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Despite being engaged by both banks and the Police, the victim remained unconvinced that the person was a scammer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: He subsequently even attempted to borrow money from his parents to fund the "investment".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It took multiple attempts by the Police before he was convinced.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These are but two examples of the cases of victims that the Police have encountered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In these cases, the Police and the banks have no legal powers to stop the victim from making further transactions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The victim would continue to lose more money to the scammers until he or she is eventually convinced that he or she is being scammed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In some of these cases, the victims have appealed to the Government for financial assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Their loved ones – spouses, children, parents – suffer too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They often have to support the victim emotionally and financially as he deals with the loss, sometimes amounting to a lifetime of savings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These family and friends, they feel frustrated and helpless.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They wish that more could have been done to protect their loved ones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In such situations, the authorities should have powers to intervene decisively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The intent is to buy the Police more time to engage and convince the individual that he is being scammed, including through enlisting the help of his family members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: ROs will only be issued as a last resort, if all other efforts to convince the individual has failed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill defines a scammer as a person who has interacted with the scam victim substantially via remote communication, for the purposes of committing or facilitating the commission of a scam offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The MHA's policy intent in introducing the power to issue ROs is primarily to protect victims from remote scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, the Police have observed some cases where scammers introduce elements of physical interaction to strengthen the deception.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These amendments will remove ambiguity over whether ROs can be issued in such cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 3 empowers a Specified Officer to issue an RO to a bank.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In other words, an individual who is subjected to an RO will have his bank accounts, automated teller machine (ATM) facilities and credit facilities suspended.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Nevertheless, the individual will be provided access to his monies for daily living expenses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will be covered in clause 5 of the Bill, which I will elaborate on later.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Operationally, the RO will be issued to the seven Domestic Systemically Important Banks, or DSIBs in short, which account for the vast majority of consumer bank accounts in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The RO will also be issued to a non-DSIB, if there is reasonable suspicion that the victim will effect transfers to a scammer from a non-DSIB account or withdraw money from it to give it to a scammer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 4 specifies the threshold that must be crossed before an RO can be issued.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, the Specified Officer must have reason to believe that the individual will transfer money to a scammer, withdraw money and give it to a scammer or apply for drawdown from a credit facility with the intention of benefiting a scammer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, the Specified Officer must determine that the RO is necessary for the protection of the individual.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: With the amendment to remove the word "substantially" from the definition of a scammer in clause 2, the legal power to issue ROs would, technically, extend beyond remote scams to more traditional cheating cases, which involve mostly physical interactions and where the other party is known to the individual in real life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They require deeper investigation to establish if there is, indeed, an offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, in a case of cheating alleged to be committed by a real friend or real lover, it is not always clear at the outset whether a criminal offence is disclosed, unlike in remote scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Hence, the threshold to issue ROs in such cases will be higher.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A Specified Officer will only issue an RO in an exceptional case when there is clear and incontrovertible evidence that a relevant offence is disclosed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Similarly, the Specified Officer must determine that the RO is necessary for the protection of an individual.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The decision to issue an RO will be made solely by the Police, based on a holistic assessment of the facts and circumstances of each case.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: While the wishes of the individual and his family members may be taken into consideration, the Police will make the final decision.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: MHA is mindful of the need to strike a balance between protecting an individual from further harm and not unduly inconveniencing him.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill takes this into consideration and has put in place four sets of safeguards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, clause 4 of the Bill requires that an RO be issued only if necessary for the protection of the victim.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: An RO is, thus, issued as a last resort.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Where there are still other options available for protecting the victim, the Police will first explore these options.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Police are notified by the bank that a person is making large transactions to an account linked to a love scammer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Despite multiple engagements by the Police, the victim refuses to believe the Police and continues to make transfers to the scammer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As part of their engagements with the victim, the Police find out that the victim has a sibling whom he is close to and he trusts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A Specified Officer may not issue an RO to restrict the victim's banking transactions or use of credit facilities, if the victim and the sibling agree to an arrangement where the sibling will monitor the victim's transactions via a joint account and can advise the victim against making further transfers to the scammer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This provides assurance that the restrictions will not be imposed for longer than is necessary to protect the individual, while ensuring that the Police have sufficient time to further engage and convince the individual.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: During this period, the Police may work with the individual's friends or family members and gather further evidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The individual may also be referred to a counsellor or a social service agency for support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A Specified Officer may cancel the RO ahead of the 30-day limit if the officer assesses that the individual is no longer at risk of making money transfers to the scammer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The RO will not be extended further, even if the victim is still at risk of transferring more money to the scammer and may well do so after the restriction order lapses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We cannot handhold the victim indefinitely, nor do we have the resources to do so, but we will do all that we can, while the RO is enforced, to bring the individual to his senses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Third, clause 5 empowers a Specified Officer to vary the RO temporarily to allow the individual to have access to the money in his bank accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, upon application by the individual, a Specified Officer will allow him to withdraw a fixed amount of money for the purposes of daily living or to pay medical bills or insurance premiums.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Fourth, clause 7 provides for an appeal process so that an individual can appeal against the issuance of an RO to the Commissioner of Police, whose decision is final.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Given that the RO will remain active pending the assessment of the appeal, MHA will ensure that the appeal process is expeditious.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: MHA has conducted public consultations on the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Around 90% of the respondents expressed support for the proposals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Some recounted past experiences, where their family members or friends were scammed and commented that the RO would have been useful in those situations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A minority of the respondents, however, highlighted the need to respect individual autonomy and were concerned that such powers would be intrusive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As I explained earlier, the RO will only be issued temporarily and only as a last resort.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Specified officers would have conducted investigations to satisfy themselves that the individual is indeed being targeted by a scammer and would have futilely engaged the individual before issuing the RO.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We will also put in place safeguards to ensure that the powers are used judiciously.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The cost of falling prey to scams does not only affect the scam victim.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Often times, their family members and even Government finances are needed to support scam victims in the aftermath.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We thus have a collective responsibility to protect potential scam victims.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This Bill allows the Police to act decisively and close a gap in our arsenal against scammers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: While this Bill alone may not significantly dent the total number of scams, it will save some individuals and their loved ones much agony and pain.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I hope the Members of this House will support the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: But even as we continue to work on providing protection to scam victims, we must remember that scam prevention and mitigation is not the responsibility of the Government alone, nor can we succeed alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Combating scams requires the whole-of-society, and we must all continue to work together to protect ourselves and our loved ones from scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such scams exploit an individual’s respect for authority, human desires and longing for companionship and love.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In some cases, the victims were so taken in by the scammers’ deceit that they refused to believe that they were being scammed, despite being repeatedly advised by their family, the banks or the Police.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Police and the banks have no legal powers to stop victims from making further transfers, so victims may continue to transfer money to scammers until they finally realise that they have been scammed, or until they have lost their life savings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Not only are the victims affected, their families, spouses, children and parents may also need to support the victims financially and emotionally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In some of these cases, families have to appeal to the Government for financial assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The authorities need the powers to intervene decisively, which is why the introduction of the Protection from Scam Bill is necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This Bill allows the Police to step in and stem further scam losses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Through ROs, if there is reason to believe that an individual will transfer money to a scammer, the Police can work with the banks to restrict the individual's banking transactions and use of credit facilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The RO will only be issued as a last resort, after all other efforts to convince the individual have failed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: During this period, the Police will work with the individual’s friends or family to gather more evidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The individual may also be referred to a counsellor or social service agency for support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We believe that this Bill is necessary as it enables us to stem scam losses and prevent scam victims from losing their life savings due to a moment of impulse or fear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But I have some clarifications to ensure it works as intended.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Imagine if someone's life savings were on the line.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Scams today do not target one person – they hit hundreds, sometimes thousands, at once.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Yio Chu Kang, I have had residents come to me, frustrated that their cases have not been followed up for weeks, even after the Police assured them that they would.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps this is a symptom of the system being overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Delays like these can erode trust in our ability to protect victims.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And what if the wrong account gets blocked?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How quickly can we fix them, so that innocent people are not left stranded?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we do more to educate the public?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us turn them into scam-fighters who can protect themselves and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, Sir, the appeals process in clause 7 is critical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many seniors in Yio Chu Kang do not even use smartphones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If their account gets blocked, how can they appeal?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Community networks, like grassroots organisations, must step up to help them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While that saves time, what about those who struggle to explain their case in writing?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To build trust, could we introduce regular reviews?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Or publish anonymised outcomes to show that the system is working fairly?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, this Bill places heavy responsibilities on banks, and rightly so.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we must be careful not to overwhelm them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is not always easy to distinguish a scam from a legitimate transaction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we provide clear guidelines, training or support, especially for smaller banks?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us work closely with banks to stop scams before they happen.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many originate overseas, where our laws have no jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could Singapore lead efforts to create a regional task force?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A shared intelligence system could make it harder for these syndicates to operate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What if we built a global registry of known scam accounts?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could help authorities and financial institutions block scammers faster.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And while clause 9 protects banks acting in good faith, we must ensure this does not lead to complacency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Especially for overseas transactions, we cannot leave any gaps.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, it is also highly intrusive, as it temporarily removes personal agency by restricting access to accounts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Temporarily freezing someone's account is a serious measure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It should only be justified by the need to protect vulnerable individuals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To mitigate this, we must prioritise robust training and resources for bank employees and artificial intelligence (AI) systems to minimise errors in account restrictions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A streamlined, human-centered appeals process is also vital to address disputes swiftly and fairly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must also be mindful of unintended consequences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Victims who feel unsupported might turn to unsafe alternatives, like loan sharks, out of desperation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, disputes involving family members over money can escalate and create long-lasting tensions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Neutral support systems, such as community networks and counsellors, must be in place to guide victims and help them recover from such experiences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For many seniors, the impact of scams goes beyond financial loss.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They often suffer a loss of dignity and confidence, leaving them too ashamed to seek help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In some tragic cases, falling prey to scams has led to severe mental health issues and even suicide.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To truly protect Singaporeans, we must act fast, be fair and address the root causes of scams.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Loneliness, financial insecurity and lack of support create vulnerabilities that scammers exploit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These underlying issues must also be tackled to build resilience in our society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It must protect the most vulnerable segments of our society, while ensuring interventions are timely, precise and carefully managed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Together, we can create a society where scams find no foothold and every resident feels safe, supported and empowered to protect themselves and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Behind some of these numbers are residents of Aljunied Group Representation Constituency, a number of whom have sought my help to recover their hard-earned money.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Sadly, in most cases I have seen, recovery has been minimal as the funds have been transferred out of Singapore and the burden of preventing scams still rests heavily on the shoulders of the end-users.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Protection from Scams Bill is an important step forward towards combating this scourge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, it introduces a significant change to the legal relationship between banks and their customers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Traditionally, banks have acted as fiduciaries with a singular duty of loyalty to their customers, including following specific instructions for financial transactions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This Bill, however, empowers the Police to issue Restriction Orders to banks, enabling them to temporarily restrict an individual's banking transactions if there is a reasonable belief that the customer is about to transfer money to a scammer.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I believe that this is a justifiable shift, given the grave risks posed by scams, including the potential for victims to lose their life savings.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, its effectiveness is contingent upon timely identification and intervention by the authorities, which may not be feasible in all cases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many scams are executed within minutes, even seconds, leaving no time for third parties to intervene.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This makes the Bill less effective in these increasingly common high-speed scenarios.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To better combat scams, we need more systemic safeguards that stop scams before they start, hold financial institutions, telecommunications companies, social media companies and messaging providers more accountable in preventing scams from taking place on their platforms and compensate victims if they fail to put in place adequate measures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, SRF focuses solely on phishing scams that lead to unauthorised transactions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It assigns a few specific duties to banks and telecommunications companies to mitigate such scams and requires compensation for victims when these duties are not fulfilled.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While SRF improves protections against phishing-related threats, it does not cover the full range of scams affecting consumers today.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many scams, such as investment scams or romance scams, rely on social engineering to deceive victims into authorising payments under false pretences.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Unlike phishing scams, these involve victims being misled about the purpose of the transaction, rather than unauthorised access.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This presents an inherent conflict of interest, as banks are both the investigator and an interested party with a financial incentive to conclude that they met their obligations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This also creates a significant disadvantage for scam victims who lack access to key evidence, such as system logs or fraud detection records and often do not have the expertise to effectively challenge the bank's findings.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Consider this scenario: a bank customer falls victim to a phishing scam, where their funds are fraudulently transferred out of their account.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The customer raises a claim under SRF, asserting that the bank failed to meet its obligations, such as sending real-time notifications or flagging a suspicious transaction through its fraud detection systems.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The bank conducts the initial investigation and concludes that it fulfilled all its duties under SRF, including providing the required alerts and adhering to the cooling-off period.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It informs the customer of its findings and denies reliability for the losses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The customer, lacking access to system logs or detailed evidence of the bank's actions, is unable to independently verify whether these obligations were indeed fulfilled.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Although the customer has the option to escalate the matter to the Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre (FIDReC) or the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), these bodies may also face limitations in their ability to access critical evidence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If these bodies are called upon to adjudicate disputes or review banks' investigations under SRF, do they have direct access to the necessary evidence, such as system logs, fraud detection records and notification timestamps?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If these bodies rely solely on banks to supply this evidence, there is a risk that the information provided may be selective or incomplete, especially when the findings could impact the bank's liability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For oversight to be truly effective, these adjudicating bodies must have the authority and technical capability to directly access and verify evidence rather than depend on the banks' representations alone.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Without this, the impartiality and robustness of the review process may be compromised.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This body would examine evidence provided by the bank, the customer and any relevant third-parties to ensure impartiality and transparency.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such a body would act as a neutral arbiter, removing the inherent conflict of interest in having banks investigate cases where they are the interested party.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, victims should be informed of their rights and available recourse options as part of the investigation outcome report.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This includes clear guidance on how to escalate disputes to independent bodies, such as FIDReC.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Providing this information upfront will ensure victims are aware of their options and are not left without avenues for redress if they disagree with the findings of the investigation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These complement the proposals I put forward in my speech during the Second Reading debate on the Online Criminal Harms Bill on 5 July 2023.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A recurring scam that my residents have brought to my attention involves the misuse of digital wallets, like Apple Pay and Google Pay.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Scammers set up a digital wallet linked to the victim's bank account.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While multi-factor authentication is typically required during set-up, scammers exploit social engineering techniques to manipulate victims into unknowingly approving the setup.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Once the wallet is linked, subsequent payments often bypass additional authentication, allowing scammers to rapidly deplete funds without further victim involvement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This highlights several possible vulnerabilities in the current system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, the reliance on multi-factor authentication alone is insufficient when victims are tricked into authorising fraudulent setups.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, once the digital wallet is authorised, there is a lack of effective monitoring to detect and flag suspicious transactions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, the absence of clear accountability between banks and digital wallet providers exacerbates the issue, leaving victims with little recourse.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These algorithms should integrate behavioural analysis, such as device changes, unusual transaction patterns or foreign Internal Protocol (IP) addresses, to flag high-risk activities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will enable proactive intervention to block unauthorised activities before the funds are lost.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Financial institutions should be required by the regulator to enhance back-end fraud detection by integrating account data, behavioural analysis and anomaly detection to identify high-risk payees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are the possible scammers or their agents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This approach minimises reliance on customers' judgement alone and strengthens fraud detection.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many platforms, including social media, email and messaging services, as well as telecommunications companies and mobile handsets already offer mechanisms to block and report suspected scams.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, these reports are often siloed, remaining on the user's device or with the platform concerned.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There is no centralised scam database to consolidate and share this information.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Currently, many scam reports only enter the scam database managed by the Singapore Police Force (SPF) if the user installs the ScamShield app and submits a scam through it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This approach is insufficient to crowdsource the collective knowledge of a broader pool of users to identify and report scams as they emerge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These platforms should then use this shared data for monitoring and proactively blocking scams on their own platforms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To promote accountability and incentivise improvements, these ratings should be clear, fair and standardised, with transparency to consumers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, vulnerabilities identified during the assessment should not be publicly disclosed until the entities have had a reasonable opportunity to address them to ensure security is not compromised.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This Bill takes an important step forward with its focus on "emergency brakes" to mitigate harm in individual cases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To effectively combat scams, we need more systemic safeguards that address root causes and build resilience across platforms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These systemic safeguards include, deploying real-time fraud detection for digital wallet transactions, enhancing Know Your Payee mechanisms to flag suspicious payees and creating a centralised scam database accessible to banks, telecommunications companies and social media companies for real-time monitoring and blocking.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Together, these measures will ensure more robust prevention, swift enforcement and shared responsibility in protecting Singaporeans from scams.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Scam cases have become more rampant in recent years.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Despite the government and banks' continuous public education activities and measures to protect bank accounts, the number of victims voluntarily transferring money to scammers remains high.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is worrying is that some victims still insist on transferring money to scammers despite the scams being exposed by relatives, friends, bank employees, or even the police on the spot.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this case, I support the Protection from Scams Bill by the Ministry of Home Affairs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The effectiveness of the bill depends on the police's quick response and investigative capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, given the eroding distinction between fraud and scams, I wonder whether the definition of scams covered by the Bill alone is sufficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, in light of how the Bill represents a significant intrusion into private transactions, I wonder if there is room to further constrain the specific application of ROs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Fraud, for them, is a result of deception.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A malicious actor obtains personal information without the victim's knowledge or consent and proceeds to use said information for financial gain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As observers, we are often inclined to place the blame for fraud on the provider and scams on the consumer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, we think of how financial institutions or telecommunications companies (telcos) can step up their surveillance of fraudulent schemes or ads, or to plug security holes in their back-end systems, or to contain fraudulent activity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has, indeed, been the focus of the SRF, where guidelines underscore how the duties and responsibilities of the bank or telco tend to be limited to actions taken when fraudulent activity is detected and ascertained.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If the consumer subsequently authorises the transaction, however, then these institutions tend to be absolved of their share of any losses since they would have already taken reasonable steps to stop said transaction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is often less sympathy for those who fall victim to scams.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many claim that victims are either too naive, or too greedy, or too careless.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Surely, if they had simply stepped back and thought through the moment more carefully, they would not fall prey to wily scammers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or worse, they are frequently viewed as willing, if unwitting, participants who should be punished to learn their lesson.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They need to recognise that 20-year-olds who connect with 80-year-olds, if they truly are even 20-year-olds, are not really there because of true love, or that it is not possible to double your money in the span of a few months by lending it to a cash-strapped entrepreneur, returns guaranteed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Those holding credit or debit cards may have inadvertently used them at a terminal with a skimmer installed or exposed their card to radio frequency identification (RFID) devices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The card then gets cloned and the clone is either used directly to make purchases or the relevant information is sold on the dark web.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Syndicates have also become sophisticated in testing the waters, effecting one or two small transactions that could easily have been missed in a sea of transactions or by sending packages to the actual address.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Verified "live" cards are then used for large purchases, usually in foreign jurisdictions with weak scammer laws.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Has the consumer truly been defrauded here, as one could argue, since they never approved these purchases?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or is it more akin to a scam since it could be argued that their indifference in response to the testing of transactions implies their acquiescence to the larger scheme?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As another example, consider an investment scam disseminated as an ad through a social media platform.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The scammer would have paid for the ad – and in many cases, an ad that is targeted at a potentially vulnerable demographic – and the text of the ad may well include disclaimer language about the "opportunity".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Surely someone who "invests" in, say, a villa in Cambodia or a business in Thailand understands the associated risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But these scammers do not always propose overt gambles of this nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: From the vantage of the social media platform, these may well seem legitimate and, unsurprisingly, the social media company would have a financial interest to classify them as such.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, when revealed to be a scam, the provider is often reluctant or outright refuses to take down the ad.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It exploits the victim's desire to secure a good deal or a job, which makes it closer to a scam.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, it embeds elements of deception, such as hidden fine print or bait-and-switch tactics, which makes them more akin to fraud.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, there is yet another third possibility often cited by defenders of the status quo – that scammers may pose as victims to try to defraud financial institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But what if the line between collaborating to deceive and a plea for assistance is far less clear?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We are certainly acquainted with cases where in the name of love or compassion, someone is asked to help with hospital expenses for a friend or their child.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Is this a scam, or a cry for help, or something in between?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While it is an empirical question whether such activities are actually as widespread as feared, or would become so if a more robust consumer protection framework were put in place, it is nevertheless true that practices of this nature tend to blur the line between scams and fraud and the sort of give-and-take that is common to human relationships.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The artificial line between frauds and scams therefore places an even more pressing onus on the formulation of laws that adequately protect Singaporeans from the scourge of both.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should not simply default to the necessary – but absolutely insufficient – calls for consumers to simply exercise more cyber hygiene while standing pat with more robust legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can cross-reference this against the guidelines issued by the Sentencing Advisory Panel for scam-related offences, which touch on sections 51 and 55A of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes Act, sections 8A and 8B of the Computer Misuse Act, and section 420 of the Penal Code.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we treat this as encompassing the full scope of how scams will be addressed by this proposed law, then the sort of scams that would trigger the issuance of restriction orders are those associated specifically with cheating behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The key question, then, is whether this definition is sufficient for prosecuting the sort of scams experienced in the real world, given the examples I have cited above.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, as already mentioned, scams could be designed such that the fraud intent is either not immediately evident or is somehow justifiable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Love, job and investment scams could be framed as genuine pursuits, with the perpetrator even undertaking actions, such as disclaimers to risky investments, or a nominal amount of useless training, or providing a genuine medical bill, that would justify the request for money and its subsequent transfer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, the most successful scams often involve confidence-building measures that exploit known weaknesses in human psychology or emotion to an extent that the scam victims may even refuse to acknowledge or believe that they are being duped even when the scam may appear evident to external parties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Undoubtedly, this is one of the focuses of the present Bill, yet many remain well in denial after the fact or refuse to face losses head-on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If an individual truly wishes to proceed with an action even when confronted with evidence to the contrary, is this indeed something that constitutes cheating?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When even experts and professionals that do this for a living may be duped, how can we be assured that the Police will have special insight or clarity, in advance, into what does or does not constitute a scam?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will the RO only be activated when the Police is able to successfully peg the case to a known scammer or organisation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we accept this inherent uncertainty, how will we be certain that ROs will also be effective in circumstances where scammers are not immediately recognised, especially in an age of AI, where the online signature of a potential scammer may easily be masked by extreme personalisation and customisation, otherwise known as "deep phishing"?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would the knowledge that a scammed victim plans to remain resolute in their insistence on a monetary transfer ultimately undermine the good-natured intent of the law?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, existing laws and regulations are always going to be somewhat incomplete, which is precisely why efforts like the current Bill are necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if we focus more narrowly on the notion of fraud, the existing framework offers scant protection for the consumer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is a matter that the Workers' Party has previously spoken up about.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, we believe that the way the SRF doles out the burden for dealing with fraud and scams remains incomplete at best, and ineffectual, at worst.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, the responsibilities of telcos in the SRF are currently only limited to texts via SMSes, perhaps due to known vulnerabilities in that system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, I am sure that many of us have received calls from what appears to be local numbers, phishing for details in a foreign accent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If indeed these are locally registered numbers rather than spoofed ones and these numbers have previously been reported to ScamShield, could the Police use registration documentation to preemptively pursue these scammers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, scams are often disseminated via alternative communications channels, such as WhatsApp messages, social media post or ads, as mentioned previously, and direct messages on social media platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, while phishing texts that seek to prod potential victims into clicking malicious links or fake websites do indeed exist, the more nefarious scamming attempts of late are reliant on social engineering and establishing relationships – much more scam than fraud.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These include instituting cooling-off periods, real-time notifications of risky transactions, a self-reporting tool for freezing accounts and a fraud detection system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These are, surely, valuable measures, but they cannot cover reasonable eventualities where the customer does not appear to be very much at fault at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One example, based on an experience that I believe many in this House would share, is when a resident encounters an unrecognised transaction in their account.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Typically, when they discover such charges on their credit card or debit card, they would simply call the bank.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The institution would typically freeze the card, issue a new one and perform an investigation into the matter, after which, in most instances, the errant transaction would be struck off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unfortunately, when the charge is on a debit card, things get far more complicated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In principle, such transactions would have required some sort of additional personal identification number (PIN) verification, which would make fraud far more unlikely.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the rise of contactless payments, as mentioned by my friend Mr Gerald Giam, means that the embedded RFID chip in the card performs the same security function, which negates the need for any additional PIN.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has permitted fraud of this nature to emerge via RFID skimming.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the cardholder could certainly take additional steps to protect their phone or cards from such skimming attempts, to me, it is a stretch to claim that the fault solely lies with the customer and that they should bear the full burden of such unauthorised transactions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As another example, consider how many banks deal with unrecognised transactions that are reported.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The process will usually entail a freeze and an investigation, as I explained earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am sure Members will also have residents who have reported erroneous transactions expeditiously – only to be subsequently told that the appeal was unsuccessful and that they would need to carry the cost of these charges even if they had no clue as to how they incurred them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a final example, think about how often we receive calls from individuals claiming to be officers from a legitimate financial institution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These days, many such calls are fraudulent and seek to illegitimately obtain the accountholder's personal information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But when customers do not have telephone banking set up, they are often asked a series of security questions, in lieu of the passcode or PIN.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if these questions do not rely on the NRIC, which, as the recent Bizfile fiasco has demonstrated, is clearly insecure, the answers to these questions may potentially be obtained by any sufficiently motivated investigator.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And on the flip side, it is far from clear how, as customers, we can verify that the caller is indeed from a financial institution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have, on more than one occasion, challenged an actual call from an officer from my bank and the absence of equivalent mechanisms to verify the legitimacy of the caller was made amply clear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What more scams, which are much more sophisticated in design and target the most vulnerable among us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, there is clearly much more work to be done to protect consumers and, hence, the driving motivation for this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, there are reasons to have reservations about the manner by which the proposed Bill goes about the task.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One may be uncomfortable, specifically, with how the Bill grants law enforcement an enormous amount of latitude to intervene and restrict what is, ultimately, a private transaction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While there is no perfect solution and, to be clear, I recognise the well-meaning nature of what is embedded in the Bill, I wonder if the law could also exercise flexibility in its application.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, is it possible for banks to offer individuals the right to designate a trusted administrator, perhaps, a close friend or relative, the full authority to freeze transactions for up to 30 days, in lieu of the Police?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill we are debating today is a groundbreaking one.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If passed, we could be the first country in the world to allow the Police to restrict bank accounts and an individual's banking transactions, if there is reasonable belief that the individual will make money transfers to a scammer.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These safeguards can include a 30-day period before the opting out takes effect, the opting out must be done in person and after a compulsory counselling session.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Additionally, an RO may run the risk of pushing emotionally-vested victims into desperation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, a victim of a romance scam may be emotionally devastated if they are prevented from sending money to the scammer, who has also become their lover.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How does the Police intend to support such victims?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party's (PSP) suggestion is for an explicit provision to be added to clause 4(b) that the Police must take into account the views of a social worker before issuing the RO.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Scam victims should be counselled by a social worker and be provided mental health support.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the assistance of family members, the social worker can determine whether an RO would be to the victim's benefit or might instead cause harm.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would better help the Police decide whether an RO would benefit the victim.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP would like to raise several further clarifications about the Bill.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has said that it will put in place a mechanism for an individual who is the subject of an RO to have access to his monies for legitimate reasons, such as sustaining daily living and paying bills.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will this mechanism be extended to all RO subjects automatically, or will they have to submit appeals to withdraw monies for legitimate reasons?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it is the latter, can the Police consider streamlining the mechanism, because it is likely that almost all RO subjects will submit such an appeal?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: RO subjects may face significant hardship if they are unable to access their money for legitimate reasons for an extended period.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Additionally, how will the Police determine the quantum of these withdrawals?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How much proof will the Police require the individual to show?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Police also subject these monies to restrictions or monitor whether individuals are also sending these withdrawals to scammers?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, will the RO extend to joint accounts owned by the individual?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, while this may protect the other joint account holder from financial losses caused by another joint account holder who is being scammed, we must also ensure that there are mechanisms to avoid unduly inconveniencing joint account holders.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the public consultation by Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH), members of the public suggested that individuals should be allowed to continue with General Interbank Recurring Order (GIRO) payments, including bill payments to legitimate organisations, while an RO is in force.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has said that the banks are unable to exempt selected transactions, such as GIRO payments and bill payments, from the RO, without significant system changes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, a freeze on such legitimate payments may add to the inconvenience and confusion faced by scam victims during an already difficult time.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, they may face financial penalties for any late or unsuccessful payment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We urge the Government to work with the banks to set up the system changes and enact this suggestion as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, the Protection from Scams Bill being read the second time today is an unprecedented piece of legislation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Once passed, we may become the first country in the world to allow the Police, under reasonable circumstances, to restrict bank transactions to prevent fraud.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that the intention behind this Bill is good.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, scam cases have been on the rise and it is necessary for us to take to strong measures to protect our citizens from the threats posed by scams.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, PSP also believes that the money in the bank accounts belongs to the users as their assets.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An important principle of private property rights is that users have the right to decide how to dispose of their assets.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To uphold this important principle, PSP proposes that we should establish an opt- out clause, allowing bank users to opt out of this restriction.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To ensure that users are not invoking this opt-out clause under the influence of scammers, we propose setting a 30-day cooling off period.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The opt-out clause would only take effect 30 days after the user invokes it, during which time the Police can restrict bank accounts to prevent fraud.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, Restriction Orders (Ros) may drive some emotionally vested victims to desperation, for example, victims of romance scams who are forcibly prevented from remitting money to their lovers may make impulsive or foolish choices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How does the Police plan to provide such support?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope that after the implementation of this Bill, we can prevent more people from voluntarily transferring money to scammers, thereby reducing Singapore’s attractiveness to scammers. : Sir, a whole-of-society effort is required to prevent the scourge of scams from spreading.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government can only do so much to protect Singaporeans from scams.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Joint account holders of scam victims are also affected by these measures.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While the intent of the proposed law is to protect individuals from losing their money, the law also grants very wide-ranging powers to the Specified Officers as they are defined at clause 2 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My first question for the Minister of State is, on the experience of these Specified Officers as defined at clause 2, they presently include any Police Officer or Commercial Affairs Officer as defined under the Police Force Act 2004.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Since the Bill grants these Specified Officers very wide-ranging and serious powers, and these are powers that impinge greatly on the personal autonomy of scam victims, can the Minister of State elaborate on the expected qualifications of these Specified Officers?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, will there be a minimum work experience requirement for these officers?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Will they be required to undergo specialised training before assuming their roles?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In her speech earlier, the Minister of State referred to certain safeguards being put in place.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister of State explain how the public can be reassured that ROs will only be issued by experienced and qualified officers?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The definition of a scam victim as provided in clause 2 of the Bill includes an individual against whom a scam offence is intended to be committed.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, my second question to the Minister of State is this: can the Ministry provide some examples of what would make a Specified Officer think that a scam victim will act in the manner as described in clause 4(1)(a)?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While the Minister of State referred to incontrovertible evidence that the scam has taken place but, if for example, no actual financial loss has taken place, how will the Specified Officer be satisfied or have reason to believe that the acts in clause 4(1)(a) of the Bill will actually take place?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Clause 4(1)(b) states that ROs may be issued when necessary to protect scam victims.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This provision takes into account the time that is required by Specified Officers, relatives, or other persons to implement preventative measures.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, it is hoped that these measures will mitigate the risks of victims continuing to fall prey to scam-related offenses.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Clause 4 (1)(b)(ii) also refers to "all other relevant circumstances" being taken into consideration.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is no indication in the Bill as to what these circumstances might be.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As the Bill already gives very wide powers to Specified Officers, could the Minister provide some more examples of the kinds circumstances that are envisaged here?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The criteria for issuing ROs seems to rely heavily on the judgment of Specified Officers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The exercise of this discretion really does need to be guided by very clear regulations to ensure that we do not see errors in judgement being committed or even worse, an abuse of power.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: What would the recourse be if the parent of a scam victim wishes to be involved in the risk mitigation measures outlined in clause 4(1)(b) of the Bill?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Can they or can they not be involved in these processes?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My fifth question has to do with the amount of time that will be taken for the consideration of an appeal against an RO.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The explanatory statement to the Bill acknowledges that there is a need to ensure that appeals are made and determined expeditiously, but is the Minister able to provide an indication on the length of time that the Commissioner will take to review an appeal?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My sixth question is on the appeals process laid out in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: At clause 7(4)(b) we see that appeals against decisions related to ROs can be decided without a hearing and in the absence of the scam victims themselves.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The absence of a formal hearing denies individuals the opportunity to present their case or to challenge evidence.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Victims or affected individuals might also feel disenfranchised by an appeals process that does not allow them to participate actively.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In light of these concerns, could the Minister clarify why clause 4(b) is required?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister also explain or provide examples of the kinds of circumstances that will result in an appeal being decided without a hearing?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My final question has to do with what the Government is doing to address the underlying causes of the perpetuation of scams.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While the Protection from Scams Bill is a blunt tool that curtails the freedoms of scam victims, ROs may also not be extended indefinitely.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The very fact that this law is required is testament to the core problem at hand and, that is, why are we in Singapore so susceptible to scams in the first place?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It has been reported quite widely that scammers manipulate victims into making poor decisions by using deep-seated psychological tactics.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They often use strategies that exploit fundamental human emotions, such as the desire for love and friendship or the instinct to make quick and guaranteed financial gains, whether through jobs or investments.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These are all very powerful motivators that can override rational thinking.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Many Members in the House had spoken about these factors but I would like to approach the matter from a slightly different perspective and, here, I would like to take the opportunity to remind the House that art can really be a very powerful tool In addressing the root causes behind the perpetuation of scams.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, it can be used to raise better awareness about scams; and secondly, it can help people to form communities of trust and care that they can lean on, instead of becoming easy prey for scammers looking to exploit their emotional vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In last year's Motion on Building an Inclusive and Safe Digital Society, I mentioned the example of HSBC in Hong Kong, which organised an art exhibition aimed at promoting public awareness on fraud prevention and online scams.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Eyeyah's resources are completely free for Singapore educators and it uses creative approaches to demystify up to 13 different scam types.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The publication includes interactive activities, such as word searches and mazes, and encourages readers to slow down and make observations.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, educators from any institution may request an e-book version to distribute schoolwide.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I am so incredibly heartened to see this successful collaboration and the important recognition given by the Government to the power of the arts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the Ministry can continue to engage more with the arts community in its educational outreach on scam prevention.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They help us to forge new social connections as well as recapture ones that may have been lost.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There are plenty of reports and statistics on this and I will highlight just one for today.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is just one example of how social engagement through the arts can be particularly effective in countering loneliness that scammers often seek to exploit when they are targeting their victims.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Crowds gathered to view the show, share their support and engage with the works on display.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The event organised by Art Outreach and Ambulance Wish, who worked very hard over Christmas and New Year breaks, brought together practising artists and various members of the public.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It really showcased how art can create a strong sense of community and shared purpose.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The atmosphere of solidarity and connection at the show was really just as moving as the art itself.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Events like this highlight how the arts can do more than just combat isolation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They build networks of care, trust and empathy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: By fostering meaningful relationships and creating environments where people look out for one another, art strengthens social bonds.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This makes individuals more resilient to scams and manipulation, which often prey on those who are isolated and who lack a supportive community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: When people feel connected and cared for, they are less likely to fall victim to exploitation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To put it another way, a community which is rooted in care and connection is one that is so much harder to exploit.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the Government will consider my suggestions for a deeper and more meaningful involvement of the arts community in our broader collective fight against scams.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my suggestions and clarifications, Sir, I support this Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given the extensive impact and losses of scam cases in Singapore, I am supportive of the introduction of the Protection from Scams Bill, which will enable the Police to better protect targets from ongoing scams who refuse to believe that they are being scammed.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nevertheless, I believe that the protection of individuals from scam should not solely rest on the Government, but there is a shared effort by the financial institutions, telecommunication companies and the public at large, in minimising the likelihood for people to fall prey to scam tactics.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will raise considerations on three key aspects of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
