text: First, on the scope of the ROs to support effective implementation; secondly, on how the Government needs to balance between safeguarding individuals' assets with fostering shared responsibility; and finally, on strategies to minimise unintended consequences, such as efforts in reducing inconvenience, maintaining public trust and enhancing public awareness.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Bill currently only allows for the issuance of ROs for scam cases conducted substantially via digital or telecommunication channels.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, scammers today have become innovative in exploiting newer platforms, such as cryptocurrency exchanges, remittance companies or e-commerce and e-wallet providers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Scams involving crypto assets are also not easily recovered as the asset can be quickly transferred overseas, with limited jurisdiction oversight, from Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This makes it easy for scammers to use such for anonymous transactions to untraceable accounts in their scam exploits.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, remittance services also play a role in cross-border scams, such as the recent investigations into the suspected fraudulent transactions by a remittance company operating in Chinatown.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Without restricting potential victims access to these platforms might result in scammers shifting their operations from traditional banking transfers to the use of crypto-assets or remittance services, for example.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, what mechanism could be in place to ensure the adaptability of the Bill in protecting victims when scammers shift to less-regulated financial platforms to conduct their scams?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The key aspect of this Bill is to protect the victims through empowering Police Officers to issue ROs to banks in Singapore to prohibit certain bank transactions and the use of credit facilities temporarily.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I support the issuance of ROs to protect individuals from losing their money to scammers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As scam victims are often manipulated or pressured into acting against their own interests, such intervention can help prevent further harm.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Bill seeks to safeguard individuals from scams, there are practical concerns about the balance between protecting victims and respecting their autonomy.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, making decisions for victims, especially before a thorough investigation can be initiated, could lead to the possibility of misjudgement for ROs to be applied.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that an RO can be issued if there is a reasonable belief that the individual will make money transfers to the scammer.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be thresholds for evidence or is the judgement based on an Officer's discretion?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, if the Police are unable to convince a potential victim to halt a particular transaction, should the responsibility, ultimately, rest with the individual if they fall victim to a scam?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How would MHA ensure that the issuance of an RO balance between protecting scam victims while respecting their autonomy and personal responsibility?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also hope that the Government can consider expanding the current SRF for phishing scams to include a broader range of stakeholders and measures.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Aside from financial institutions and telecos, to include e-commerce and e-payment platforms, remittance companies and social media companies.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These entities can contribute to scam prevention by enhancing account verification process, monitoring suspicious activities and implementing robust measures to safeguard users from fraudulent schemes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additional scam types, such as malware-enabled fraud and cryptocurrency scams, should also be included in a broader framework to address evolving tactics of scammers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will allow stakeholders to robustly implement targeted measures to reduce the vulnerabilities in digital ecosystem and allow for collaborative efforts between law enforcers and technology platforms to disrupt fraudulent activities at source.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, I understand that clause 5 of the Bill allows for ROs to be in force for up to 30 days; and clause 7 provides for appeals against the decision to issue a RO.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If greater public awareness and education on Money Lock and Kill Switch can help to support the effectiveness of these safeguards, we should do more to help our Singaporeans to safeguard their assets.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Greater collaboration between financial institutions and law enforcement agencies, through public education campaigns, will be essential to maximise the impact of these tools in protecting individuals from financial harm.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that its success depends on our ability to ensure ROs are implemented effectively, strike a delicate balance in protecting individuals without overstepping into personal autonomy and responsibility and minimise unintended consequences that may burden victims while enhancing public awareness and education.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moving forward, we must adopt a collective approach, involving financial institutions, telecommunications companies, technology platforms and individuals themselves to combat scams comprehensively.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Bill must, thus, serve not only as a legal safeguard, but also inspire a broader culture of vigilance and resilience against scams.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Together, we can protect the vulnerable from the risk of scams and strengthen our society against such evolving threats.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These figures are not just numbers, they represent real people and their heartbreaking stories of retirees losing their life savings, individuals manipulated by false promises of love and people driven to financial and emotional despair.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: One recent case involved a man on the brink of losing all his $600,000 in savings, but was saved by the quick intervention by a diligent bank officer.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, not every story has a happy ending.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Even when faced with undeniable evidence, many victims remain steadfast in their trust in scammers, sometimes to their ruin.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The escalating scam landscape also poses a multifaceted threat to Singapore's business ecosystem, with small and medium enterprises particularly vulnerable to sophisticated cyber threats that can inflict severe financial, operational and reputational damage.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond direct monetary losses, businesses face increased cybersecurity investment costs, potential operational disruptions and erosion of customer trust, whilst employees handling financial transactions become prime targets for scammers seeking to compromise both personal and corporate assets.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These challenges not only jeopardise individual companies' sustainability but also undermine the broader confidence in Singapore's digital economic infrastructure, necessitating comprehensive protective strategies that extend beyond individual victim protection.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill represents a pivotal step forward, balancing the need to respect individual freedom with the collective responsibility to shield our citizens from irreparable harm.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Today, as we discuss this Bill, let us remember that this is not just legislation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It is a lifeline for those caught in the psychological grip of scammers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It reflects a commitment to safeguarding the vulnerable in our community and a testament to our determination to combat this escalating issue.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: They will allow the Police to intervene before financial damage occurs, providing a crucial window of protection for potential victims who may be transferring money to scammers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These Orders can be issued to freeze or restrict certain activities that may lead to further victimisation, such as freezing bank accounts or restricting certain financial transactions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While we recognise that implementing these measures may pose operational challenges for our financial institutions, requiring system adaptations and staff training, this investment in infrastructure will, for sure, strengthen our financial ecosystem against fraud.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, this legislation presents significant opportunities for innovation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We anticipate increased demand for advanced fraud detection and prevention technologies.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This opens new avenues for Singapore-based companies to develop cutting-edge solutions, potentially creating a new export market for our cybersecurity expertise.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Our fintech sector stands to benefit greatly, too, from these developments.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Though we need to strike a balance between regulatory effectiveness and technological innovations, I do believe stronger protections will increase public confidence in the banking and financial systems.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We must also consider the cross-border implications of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As we implement these measures, we need to ensure that they do not unduly hinder legitimate international financial relationships and cross-border transactions, which are vital to our economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The enhanced trust in a system, our well-oiled cross-border processes, coupled with a proactive stance against scams, will reinforce Singapore's reputation as a secure financial hub, potentially attracting more international investment.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: One, at this juncture, what would be the minimum threshold for issuing these Orders?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Two, could the Ministry spell out clear timelines and documentation requirements for scam victims or joint account holders appealing against the ROs?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Three, could additional details be outlined on the limits of immunity granted to banks and their staff, particularly in cases of unintentional errors?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Four, what will be the criteria and processes for including new offences to ensure transparency and consistency?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Five, could I request the Minister of State to outline the process for scam victims to apply to lift or modify restrictions, ensuring timely resolution of legitimate concerns?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, would it be useful at this time to establish a single regulatory body to coordinate the mechanisms between banks, regulatory authorities and officers to streamline the implementation of the Bill's provisions?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The importance of the Protection from Scams Bill cannot be overstated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The aim of this authority is to enable the Police to better protect targets of ongoing scams, who refuse to believe that they are being scammed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, I have four issues of concern that I would like to clarify.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Before I do, I would like to make some introductory comments to reinforce the need for these changes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to note that I am currently the head of the Public Safety and Security programme at the Singapore University of Social Sciences and cybercrime is an issue of primary concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Scamming is a crime that can and does impact people of all ages and genders and all social, cultural and economic backgrounds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: According to the World Economic Forum, digital trust is an expectation that digital technologies and services will protect the interest of their stakeholders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Scammers are aware of this trust and use increasingly sophisticated and believable psychological and emotional techniques to manipulate it in their favour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Scamming is not something that only impacts others.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Overriding the decision-making authority of a competent adult is a significant step and one that should not be taken lightly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we already have guardianship and financial management legislation to protect adults who are legally considered incompetent to make decisions in their own best interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These provisions do not, however, apply in the context of this Bill, as the adults in question are still legally competent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps guidelines need to be developed to ensure transparency and consistency in forming a view that what all reasonable attempts have been exhausted?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: My third issue relates to the training and support to be provided to bank officers to enable them to comfortably and competently recognise issues that may require intervention, determining if and when a customer is seeking to make a transaction that may be scam-related or not, in the customer's best interest, is not as straightforward as it sounds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We do not want to inadvertently create a situation where banks either over-refer or under-refer customers and, again, perhaps, guidelines need to be developed to ensure consistency in referral process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: That is, instead of banks contacting the Police, they contact a nominated community organisation, who can work with the customer to determine if an RO is actually needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Many victims of scams experience significant and ongoing issues after being or almost being scammed, including financial loss, emotional distress or trauma, relationship difficulties and housing or employment issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Ministry could establish dedicated support services to provide free and confidential support to victims or near-victims of scams, including those subjected to ROs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill addresses one of those risks and, in doing so, aims to protect the financial, social and emotional health and well-being of thousands of fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even more shocking, is the staggering amount of money lost to such scams.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is particularly troubling is the significant amounts lost in individual cases.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During the same period, government officer impersonation scams (GOIS) and investment scams stood out as the most financially devastating.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This issue is not confined to any one demographic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my conversations with residents of Pasir Ris-Punggol, I have met scam victims of GOIS, love scams and investment scams.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Contrary to popular belief, the victims are no longer just the elderly or the digitally inexperienced.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Increasingly, they include younger professionals – educated and digitally literate individuals – something which was mentioned by Assoc Prof Razwana earlier.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While the statistic that 86% of scams involved self-effected transfers may suggest a level of voluntary action, the reality, Mr Speaker, is far more insidious.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A common modus operandi involves seemingly innocuous messages, such as a notice from the Land Transport Authority claiming an underpayment of 10 cents for parking or a fine.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The message contains a link to settle the fine and while the initial transfer appears minor, it serves as a gateway for scammers to drain much larger sums from victims' accounts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She received such a message, prompting her to make a small initial payment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Shortly after, she received an alert from her bank about several overseas transactions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She immediately informed the bank that she had not authorised these transactions and was a victim of a scam.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, to her dismay, the bank allowed the transactions to proceed, citing the fact that she had already initiated the first transfer as part of an e-wallet.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a result, she lost close to $3,000.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Allow me to share another distressing case involving a Pasir Ris-Punggol resident who fell victim to a love scam.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This case came to my attention when her family, in sheer desperation, sought my assistance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The victim, a 60-year-old woman, had already transferred more than $50,000 to an overseas acquaintance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Shockingly, this sum included loans that she had taken from her own family members.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite her family's repeated efforts to intervene and persuade her to stop, she remained resolute in her actions, believing in the legitimacy of her relationship.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Her family approached me to talk to her, hoping I could help her see the gravity of the situation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This case underscores the deeply manipulative nature of scams, which prey not only on victims' financial resources, but also on their emotions and trust.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, Mr Speaker, I stand in support of this Bill, which seeks to empower the Police to issue ROs to banks, enabling them to limit banking transactions for individuals when there is reasonable belief that these funds may be transferred to scammers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is undeniably a significant step, granting the Police substantial authority over an individual's access to their own financial resources.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such powers are, by nature, intrusive and it is imperative that we approach this matter with utmost caution.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must strike a delicate balance between holding individuals accountable for their financial actions and ensuring that authorities do not overreach in matters of personal autonomy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I support the intent and direction of the Bill, I have several clarifications and concerns that I hope the Minister of State will address: firstly, on the issuance of the Restriction Order; secondly, on the scope of the RO; and thirdly, on minimising the inconvenience to individuals affected.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I seek clarification from the Minister regarding the definition of this Specified Officer.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will this Officer be the one reporting the case, the investigating officer or someone from a specialised branch of the Police Force focused on scams?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This provision grants significant authority to the Police over an individual's financial assets.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that such powers are not subject to abuse and that there is accountability in their exercise of power?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the same time, to make this measure truly effective, how do we ensure an efficient process that prevents victims from transferring further funds to scammers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the love scam case I cited earlier, the victim was rushing to transfer money and without immediate intervention, the transfer would have already been completed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As an additional safeguard, since such cases often involve family members who act as the primary complainants to the Police in their efforts to stop further transfers, should the issuance of an RO be contingent on a valid complaint lodged by a credible party, such as a family member?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, considering the significant sums often lost in scams, a penalty of $3,000 appears disproportionately small when weighted against the devastating financial impact on the victims.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition to imposing a heftier fine, I urge that banks be held liable to the victims for any losses incurred as a direct result of their failure to comply with the RO.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such accountability would ensure that banks take their obligations under this Bill seriously and act decisively to protect victims from further harm.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, there is also something that we need to address on how scam cases are investigated by the banks.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Currently, when a victim reports a fraudulent transaction, the bank handles the investigation internally and issues their findings, leaving victims with limited recourse.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To better protect victims, we should consider appointing an independent arbitrator to review such cases, ensuring a fair and transparent process for redress.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moving to my second point regarding the scope of the RO, I seek clarification on whether banks can also be mandated to halt transactions if victims explicitly acknowledge that the transactions are fraudulent.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In such cases, should banks not also bear the responsibility to recover the lost funds if they proceed with the transfer despite the victim's warning?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the first case I highlighted earlier, the victim had shared that, apparently, they had already informed the bank that the transactions were fraudulent.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, the bank allowed the transfer to proceed, citing that it was self-effected as she had already set up the e-wallet with the scammer's bank details.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This raises serious concerns about the level of accountability expected from financial institutions in safeguarding their customers, particularly in situations where fraud had already been flagged.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moving to my third point, individuals subjected to an RO may face limitations on their ability to transfer or withdraw money as well as restrictions on their credit facilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While it is mentioned that mechanisms will be in place to allow access to funds for legitimate purposes, such as daily living expenses and bill payments, this access will be determined on a case-by-case basis upon application to the Police.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that applications can take time and investigations into scam cases may span several months, I propose that the default position should be to ensure individuals affected by an RO have immediate access to sufficient funds to sustain their daily living.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would provide a safety net while investigations are ongoing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It would be deeply unfair and disproportionate to cut off an individual from their own financial resources without prior notice or a mechanism for immediate relief.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such scams are not confined to specific groups but are increasingly targeting individuals who are educated and digitally literate.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The modus operandi in scam cases is becoming more sophisticated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sometimes, they impersonate government officials, starting with fake messages, such as fines or overdue payments, which ultimately lead to much greater losses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, safeguards are needed to prevent misuse and ensure accountability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Banks must act swiftly when notified of scams and be held responsible if they fail to comply with the order.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Additionally, independent arbitrators should oversee banks' investigations into scams cases to ensure justice for victims.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This balance is important to effectively combat scams and deliver justice for scam victims. : Mr Speaker, scams not only rob individuals of their hard-earned money but also erode trust and confidence in our financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Bill is a crucial step in addressing these challenges, but it must be implemented with precision, transparency and fairness.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Safeguarding victims while balancing the powers of authority and personal autonomy is no easy task.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, by refining processes, ensuring accountability and minimising undue inconvenience to individuals, we can make meaningful strides in combating this growing threat.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I stand firmly in support of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They have raised important questions, which I will now address.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling asked if the RO could be expanded to include other entities, such as cryptocurrency exchanges, remittance companies and e-wallet providers, should scammers shift their tactics to exploit these platforms.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will continue to work with MAS to monitor the scam situation and consider expanding the scope of the Restriction Order in future, if necessary.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Neil Parekh asked about the criteria and process for including new scam offences into the Schedule to the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will consider including a new offence into the Schedule if it has nexus to scams, such as offences related to cheating or fraud.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Minister for Home Affairs can amend the Schedule to include the new offences.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Neil Parekh also asked what the minimum threshold for issuing an RO would be.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling and Ms Usha Chandradas asked how the threshold of "reasonable belief" would be established, when assessing whether an RO should be issued, renewed or cancelled.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: An RO can be issued once two conditions are satisfied.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First, there is reason to believe that the victim is likely to make a monetary transfer to a scammer, withdraw money and give it to a scammer, or apply for a draw down from a credit facility with the intention of benefiting a scammer.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Second, an RO is necessary to protect a scam victim, having regard to the time required to engage the victim and implement risk mitigation measures.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Officers will assess every case based on the specific facts and circumstances.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is what the Police are trained to do in the course of any investigation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As an example, in their assessment, the Police will consider factors such as: one, whether the victim is still in communication with a scammer; two, whether the victim has transferred monies to the scammer; three, whether the victim continues to believe the scammer; and four, whether the victim is likely to transfer money to a scammer.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked about what it means for the attempts by the Police to convince the individual having been "exhausted".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Usha Chandradas asked whether parents can be involved in the risk mitigation measures and what "other circumstances" we have in mind when determining whether an RO is required to protect the victim.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Our policy intent is for the RO to be issued as a last resort.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: By extension, this means that wherever feasible, we intend to explore other interventions first, and to only issue an RO if these other interventions fail.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These interventions could include engaging the relatives of the victim or other persons, which could include the victim's parents where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We have drafted the legal provision broadly to empower the Police to take into account the specific circumstances of the case, which can vary significantly, when making their assessments.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling asked whether the responsibility should ultimately rest with the victim, if the Police are unable to convince the victim of the scam.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Hazel Poa suggested to allow individuals to opt out of the RO regime, given that they have the right to determine the use of their monies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As I had mentioned in my opening speech, we cannot handhold the victim indefinitely.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But we will do all that we can while the RO is in force to bring the individual to his senses.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If the individual persists in making transfers to scammers after the maximum RO period, the responsibility must lie with the individual.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked if the Government would consider lowering the threshold to issue an RO, in order to minimise scam losses.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He also asked if a third party would be subject to an RO, if the third party assists an individual who is subjected to an RO to transfer monies to the scammers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Indeed, the authorities have to intervene decisively in scam cases, in order to protect the individual and minimise losses.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, imposing an RO entails causing significant inconvenience to the individual subjected to the RO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is therefore important for officers to carry out due diligence so that they can assess whether an RO is warranted and avoid, or at least minimise, the mistakes in blocking an account that Mr Yip cautioned against.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Our view is that the current threshold stipulated in the Bill is appropriate.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Officers will issue an RO if they have reason to believe that the individual will make monetary transfers to a scammer, withdraw any money and give it to a scammer, or apply for or draw down from any credit facility with the intention of benefiting a scammer.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, if the third party is also an unwitting victim of the scammer and similarly, at risk of making monetary transfers of his or her own to the scammer, then the officers may similarly consider whether that individual should be the subject of a separate RO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked how ROs can be issued in an efficient manner, such that it is effective in preventing victims from transferring further funds to scammers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We recognise that speed is of essence in preventing losses, but the Police must also conduct the necessary investigations to determine if a case has met the threshold for issuance of an RO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police will also work closely with the banks, which are co-located at the Anti-Scam Command (ASCom), in their investigations and in effecting the restrictions on the victim’s bank account.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MHA would prefer to take a risk-calibrated approach by imposing the ROs on Joint-Alternate accounts and exempting Joint-All accounts given their lower risk of being depleted through scams.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is not ideal, but we have decided to go ahead with the Bill at this juncture to provide victims with the necessary protection at the soonest.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will continue to work with the banks to explore the possibility of putting in place technical solutions to facilitate such exemptions in the future.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will notify all joint account holders should an RO be imposed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will also facilitate their access of monies in the joint accounts.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members have asked how family members of individuals would be involved and consulted when an RO is being issued, cancelled or renewed, and whether family members or banks can initiate for Police to consider issuing an RO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked if the issuance of an RO should be contingent on a valid complaint lodged by a credible party, such as a family member.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members of the public, including a victim’s family members, can make a Police report, when they suspect that an individual or their family member has encountered a scam.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police will conduct investigations and assess if an RO should be issued.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In determining whether an RO should be issued, the Police may engage the victim’s family members, to assess if there is reason to believe that the victim is being scammed, and to explore whether it would suffice for the family to intervene and convince the individual that he or she is the victim of a scam without the need for an RO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, the Police may uncover potential scam victims in the course of investigating mule accounts, or the Police may be alerted by bank staff of an individual who is suspected to be a scam victim.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For such cases, it is not necessary and may be less efficient to require a family member or other third party to file a police report.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police are required to perform due diligence checks and will issue an RO if the threshold for issuance is met.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked if a trusted friend or relative could be empowered to freeze transactions, in lieu of the Police.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Earlier in my opening speech, I had provided an example where if the victim and the sibling agree on an arrangement where the sibling will monitor the victim's transactions via a joint account and can advise the victim against making further transfers to the scammer, the Specified Officer may not issue an RO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: That said, I would like to reiterate that the decision to issue an RO will be made by the Police.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police would have been engaging with the individual and his family members for some time, and the Police will be in the best position to make an objective and informed decision.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about the estimated number of ROs that would be issued in a year and the potential losses that could have been avoided if we had implemented this earlier.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police do not currently track the number of cases where Police officers have been activated to engage potential victims, as well as the number of successful and unsuccessful interventions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The actual number will depend on the cases that are brought to the Police’s attention and their assessment of each case.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Hazel Poa and Assoc Prof Razwana noted that some victims may be emotionally affected when being prevented from sending money to the scammer and asked how the Police intend to support such individuals in course of them being subject to an RO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: She also suggested for MHA to require the Police to take into account the views of a social worker before issuing an RO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As I have mentioned, speed is of the essence in order to protect these individuals and minimise losses, which in some cases might involve all of the victim's life savings.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Hence, an RO will be issued once the Police have assessed that the conditions for an issuance is satisfied.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Notwithstanding, victims who require emotional support during the process may inform the investigation officer, who will arrange for them to speak to a victim care officer.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MHA will work with the Police on the operational details to ensure that victims are adequately supported.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I have made available copies of a pamphlet with frequently asked questions for victims of scams and avenues for them to consult mental well-being counselling and other financial assistance channels.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This copy, a resource guide, is available for Members at the entrance and exit for the Parliamentary Chamber.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members can see that there is a section called "Where can I seek support?" that directs victims to support from victim care officers and to community support in the form of mental well-being and counselling support.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Neil Parekh asked about the process for individuals to apply to lift or modify an RO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how quickly a restriction on an account can be lifted, especially if a wrong account gets blocked.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling asked if there would be mechanisms to allow an individual who is subjected to an RO to access limited funds for his daily expenses while investigations are underway.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Sharael Taha and Ms Hazel Poa suggested for an individual subjected to an RO to have immediate access to sufficient funds, instead of having to apply for it.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We understand the need to minimise inconvenience to the affected individual.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MHA and MAS are working with the banks on the operational details, including the amount of time required to impose or lift an RO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Notwithstanding, if the bank makes a mistake in complying with the RO and blocks a wrong account, the bank should rectify the mistake immediately.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Hazel Poa asked if an individual can be exempted from certain legitimate facilities, such as GIRO bill payments, or have any financial penalties arising from late bill payments waived, during the period where the RO is in effect.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Poa also asked what proof an individual would need to show for withdrawals, how will the Police determine the quantum of the withdrawals and whether the amount withdrawn would be subjected to further restrictions or monitoring.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This could include, for example, bill statements, such as for medical expenses, utility and rental payments, or any documentation as requested by the Police.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Every request will be assessed on a case-by-case basis, based on the needs of each individual.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This amount will not be subjected to further restriction or monitoring, since it has been assessed to be necessary for the individual.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MHA agrees with Ms Poa's suggestion and has, in fact, considered exempting individuals from certain legitimate facilities, such as GIRO bill payments.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, the banks have informed us that it is not feasible to exempt selected transactions from the RO without significant system changes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Again, this is not ideal but we have decided to go ahead with the Bill at this juncture, given the importance of providing victims with the necessary protection at the soonest.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But we hear your feedback and we will continue to work with banks towards allowing for these exemptions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the question of lead time required before an individual can access his funds, once the Police have assessed if the individual should be allowed access to funds, the Police will work with the banks to arrange for the individual to make the withdrawal at a bank branch.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We are working with the banks on the operational details and our intent is to ensure that this is done as quickly as possible.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Usha Chandradas and Mr Sharael Taha as well as Assoc Prof Razwana Begum had asked who the Specified Officers engaging the individuals would be, including their seniority and qualification, and how MHA would ensure that these powers are not subject to abuse.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Neil Parekh, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms Usha Chandradas asked about the documentation requirements for an appeal, how long it would take for the Commissioner of Police to review an appeal and whether hearings should be allowed for appeals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Yip also asked if the Government would conduct regular reviews on the decisions regarding appeals or publish anonymised outcomes of such appeals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I trust that Members will agree with me that our officers can be expected to perform their duties professionally and impartially.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To ensure no conflict of interest in the appeals process, appeals will be decided by the Commissioner of Police, whose decision is final.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The appeal process has been designed with speed in mind to ensure that an appeal can be decided expeditiously, issued judiciously and officers are held accountable for the exercise of this power.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MHA will prescribe in subsidiary legislation, the documents and information an individual will need to provide when submitting an appeal.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These would include, but are not limited to: one, any evidence that the individual has taken up additional safeguards willingly and, therefore, the Restriction Order is no longer required for his protection; and two, any evidence that the individual is not a target of scams, such as proof that the other party is legitimate.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On Assoc Prof Razwana's suggestion for individuals subject to an RO to be automatically referred for independent legal advice, individuals are free to seek their own legal advice and avail themselves of the appeal mechanism.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In operationalising the Bill, we will ensure that victims are adequately supported and appeals are fairly assessed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I would also like to remind Members that the Police will always try to engage the victim before deciding whether to proceed with an RO, since the RO is intended to be a lever of last resort.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, we will not have a situation where the Police decides to proceed with the RO without trying to find out the perspective of the victim first.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Neil Parekh asked about the limits of immunity granted to banks and their staff, particularly, in cases of unintentional errors.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is in line with section 35(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which is in relation to banks being ordered by the Police to seize property held in their account or safe deposit box.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Thus, it is a close approximate to the current order to freeze the bank account of the suspected scam victim.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Sharael Taha suggested for banks to be held liable for losses incurred resulting from their failure to comply with an RO, in addition to a heftier maximum fine quantum.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He also asked if banks could, additionally, be mandated to stop transactions, if informed by a victim that the transactions were fraudulent.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As I have mentioned, MHA shares the desire to minimise inconveniences for the affected individual.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, to guard against the risk of abuse, any request for funds will have to be assessed based on facts and circumstances of each case.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Should the individual request for more money, thereafter, the Police will require him to show proof of the need to access the money.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is to avoid the risk of scammers exploiting this mechanism to obtain monies from the individual.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked if the definition of scams covered by the Bill is sufficient, given that it may be difficult to distinguish between scams and traditional cheating cases.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police regard scams as cheating offences that are conducted remotely, online or over telecommunications.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Traditional cheating, on the other hand, involves mostly physical interactions, where the other party is known to the individual in real time.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: That said, however, as pointed out by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, the Police have, indeed, observed cases where scammers introduced elements of physical interaction to strengthen the deception and, hence, we have amended the Bill to ensure that the ROs can be applied in such cases.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The offences in the law include, cheating and offences under the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 and the Computer Misuse Act 1993.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These offences cover the full range of acts that constitute or facilitate scams.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And to send a stronger deterrent signal, guidelines issued by the Sentencing Advisory Panel have recommended higher sentences for acts that facilitate scams.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I will now cover other issues and suggestions from Members and as these matters fall outside the scope of this Bill, I will address them very briefly.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked if MHA would consider getting the banks to increase the number of checks required before a fund transfer can be allowed, to buy the authorities more time to engage and convince the individual.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Banks have improved their real-time fraud surveillance in detecting possible fraudulent transactions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Today, bank staff may call up their customers to verify their transactions, if suspicious activity is detected.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Cooling periods, such as those for the activation of digital tokens and other high-risk activities, will help to slow down selected transactions and give individuals more time to think about the transfers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ultimately, banks will have to balance between fraud prevention and customer experience, as they consider ways to enhance their anti-scam measures.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Assoc Prof Razwana Begum asked if the Government could provide banks with the necessary guidelines, training or support to ensure that banks are able to distinguish a scam from a legitimate transaction.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members had also asked if MHA would consider having periodic reviews of bank processes or to facilitate sharing of best practices among banks, to ensure implementation effectiveness across the board.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Neil Parekh also asked if it would be useful to establish a single regulatory body to coordinate the processes among the banks, the regulatory authorities and the officers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Gerald Giam also suggested for real-time coordination between the Police, MAS, the banks and other platforms to enhance enforcement against scams.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We welcome other stakeholders, including social media platforms, to co-locate within ASCom, to improve real-time coordination.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police also regularly share observations with banks to improve their fraud detection capabilities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This model has worked well and we will continue to build upon it to strengthen enforcement against scammers and recovery of scam proceeds.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We agree with the suggestion to facilitate the sharing of best practices amongst banks and we are considering how to do so efficiently and effectively.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling and Mr Gerald Giam raised a number of suggestions to tackle scams, including on SRF, Money Lock and Kill Switch.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These are outside the scope of the Bill and Members may wish to file Parliamentary Questions on these.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Usha Chandradas also suggested for MHA to consider including art as a tool to address the root causes behind the perpetration of scams by victims.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We note Ms Ng's and Ms Chandradas' suggestions and will take them into account, as we review our overall approach to tackle scams.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng suggested for the Government to strengthen cross-border enforcement against scams and do more to educate the public on scams.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Cross-border enforcement is indeed a priority, given the transnational nature of scams.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The new 1799 helpline, which operates 24/7, offers the public an easy option to check with whenever they are unsure if a situation they are facing is a scam.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MHA will share more on our public education initiatives at the upcoming Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The threat will keep evolving and we must ensure that we have the appropriate tools to deal with this threat, as this Bill aims to do.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will continue to evolve our methods, evolve our laws, to continue our fight against scams.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any Members have clarifications for the Minister of State?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Does the Minister of State agree that this Bill will have limited impact on combating scams overall and that more systemic safeguards are needed?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: However, I was not proposing just the sharing of best practices but sharing and collecting data from these social media platforms and requiring them to use that data to prevent scams from taking place in the first place.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, is that something that the Police are prepared to do?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I also mentioned that we require a whole-of-society effort and we will have to work with stakeholders collectively to fight the scourge of scams.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: That said, when we look at the cases we have encountered, because the cases we are targeting right now are those that involve social engineering.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And the cases I had cited – government official impersonation scams, love scams, investment scams – we have observed that the losses from these categories of scams, especially if they are over a long period of time, can lead to quite large amount of losses.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, while in terms of the number of scams that could be deterred through this Bill which we approximate to be between five and 10 cases a month, I think we should not neglect the fact that actually, the absolute amounts arising from these losses could be substantial.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And definitely, when we look at it on an individual basis, we could be talking about the loss of lifetime savings.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But that said, this is but one of many other methods and many other initiatives we are undertaking to fight the scourge of scams.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We should not downplay the importance of public education because at the end of the day, when it comes to socially-engineered scams, the best defence really is a discerning public.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Sorry, could I ask the Member to repeat the second question?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It was to seek a response to the proposal about sharing data between the banks, social media companies and the Police – so, consolidating all that crowd-sourced data to be able to prevent scams from taking place in real-time.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There is a mechanism whereby different stakeholders share trends that they observe.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The only thing I would say is that for some of the social media companies, they have certain data protection laws.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, while they have not disagreed with the sharing of information and data that they see and observe, sometimes, there is a certain lag time, because they need to process the information on their end, make sure that the information is in the form that can be shared with external parties.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Therefore, we see that there could be a lapse in terms of timing when it comes to the sharing of information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But definitely, the key principle of sharing information and data between platforms, between stakeholders to tackle the scourge of scams, that principle is something that we all collectively agree with.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The first question is, although the numbers may not be significant, would the Minister of State clarify if, in dollar terms, the Bill would have a significant impact and therefore, reduction to the current scams amount that happens every year?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The second question would be, if this takes place, in terms of this policy and if it is effective, would the Minister of State be thinking that this may be extended to other platforms, such as crypto companies and institutions of that sort, beyond banks?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We have also had a couple of outliers when we are talking about a couple of million dollars.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, it is very hard for me to be able to pinpoint a number to say that because we now have this RO regime in place that "X" amount of scam losses will be prevented every month.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: All I can say is that when we looked at the cases that the Police have encountered, when we looked at the cases that the Police have to be activated, where they have gone down, to their best efforts, together with family members and friends and try and convince scam victims that they are scam victims and still, unfortunately, the victims continued to believe that they are not scam victims – when we look at those cases, in particular, because it happens over a period of time, the losses are pretty substantial.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The citation year "2024" will be changed to "2025" as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.
